unit.title: Light
unit.blurb: Seeing, straight rays, mirrors, the Sun and the Moon, day and night, and shadows.

O1.t: Know that we need light to see, name light sources, and know that light bounces off objects into our eyes.

O2.t: Know that light travels in straight lines and cannot bend round corners.

O3.t: Know that light reflects, that shiny surfaces reflect more light, and why reflectors keep us safe.

O4.t: Know that the Sun is a star and a light source, and that planets and moons reflect sunlight.

O5.t: Explain day and night by the spinning of the Earth.

O6.t: Know that shadows form when light is blocked, and that shadow length changes during the day.

captions: Hello, light detectives!
How do our eyes see things? Let's find out.
This is lesson 5.1: how we see things.
At night, switch off all the lights.
Can you see your toys? No! It is too dark.
Now switch on the light.
Now you can see everything! We need light to see.
A light source gives out its own light.
The Sun is a light source.
A lamp, a candle and a torch are light sources too.
Pause and think.
Which of these is a light source?
How do you see a book?
Light comes from a light source, like a lamp.
The light bounces off the book.
Then the light goes into your eyes. And you see the book!
Did you know?
The Moon looks bright, but it is not a light source.
We see it because sunlight bounces off it!
Riddle time!
What can fill a whole room, but takes up no space?
Light!
Your turn.
Why can't we see anything in a completely dark room?
Let's make a dark box.
Put a toy inside a box, close the lid, and peep through a small hole.
Can you see the toy? It is too dark!
Now open a flap to let light in. What happens?
Let's remember.
We need light to see.
A light source gives out its own light, like the Sun.
Light bounces off things and goes into our eyes.
And the Moon is not a light source. Bright work!

captions: Hello, light detectives!
Light can bounce. Let's see how!
This is lesson 5.3: light reflects off surfaces.
Look in a mirror.
Hello! You can see yourself!
Light bounces off the mirror and back into your eyes.
When light bounces off something, we say it reflects.
Shiny, smooth surfaces reflect lots of light.
A mirror and a metal spoon are shiny.
Dull, rough surfaces reflect less light.
A brick and a teddy bear are dull.
Pause and think.
Which surface reflects the most light?

Light can bounce off surfaces.

Shiny, smooth surfaces reflect more light than dull ones.

captions: Hello, space explorers!
Why do we have day and night?
This is lesson 5.5: day and night.
The Earth is always spinning, like a top.
The side of the Earth facing the Sun has day.
The side facing away from the Sun has night.
As the Earth spins, day changes to night!
Pause and think.
Why do we have day and night?
The Earth takes one whole day to spin round once. That is twenty-four hours.
In the morning, the Sun seems to rise.
At midday, it is high in the sky. In the evening, it seems to set.
Then it is night time! The Sun did not move. The Earth spun round.
Did you know?
When it is daytime where you live, it is night time on the other side of the world!
Riddle time!
What seems to go up in the morning and down in the evening, but does not really move?
The Sun! It is the Earth that spins!
Your turn.
How long does the Earth take to spin round once?
Let's spin a globe!
Put a sticker on the place where you live.
Shine a torch at the globe, and spin it slowly.
When is it day for your sticker? When is it night?
Let's remember.
The Earth is always spinning.
The side facing the Sun has day.
The side facing away has night.
And one spin takes twenty-four hours. Out of this world!

q.prompt: At what time of day is your shadow shortest?

captions: Hello, shadow detectives!
Where do shadows come from?
This is lesson 5.6: investigating shadows.
Stand outside on a sunny day.
Your body blocks the sunlight.
Behind you, there is a dark patch with no light.
That is your shadow!
Pause and think.
How is a shadow made?
Shadows change during the day.
In the morning, the Sun is low, and shadows are long.
At midday, the Sun is high, and shadows are short.
In the evening, shadows are long again.
You can make shadow puppets!
Shine a torch on a wall.
Make a shape with your hands in front of the light.
Look! A rabbit shadow!
Did you know?
Long ago, there were no clocks.
People used the shadow on a sundial to tell the time!
Riddle time!
What follows you everywhere on a sunny day, but disappears at night?
Your shadow!
Your turn.
At what time of day is your shadow shortest?
Let's measure shadows.
Push a stick into the ground, in a sunny place.
Measure its shadow in the morning, at midday, and in the afternoon.
When was the shadow shortest?
Let's remember.
A shadow forms when something blocks the light.
Shadows are long in the morning and evening.
Shadows are short at midday.
So shadows change during the day. Super shadow work!
